opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think about it in terms of generality. That's always been the heart of the concept for me. When I helped popularize the term "artificial general intelligence" years ago, the point was to contrast it with narrow AI, systems that are superhuman at chess or Go but can't do anything else. So the question is whether a system can do the broad range of cognitive things that people can typically do.

In practice, I'd approach it in two stages. First, you build a big battery of tests covering the breadth of human cognition: language, reasoning, maths, planning, learning new skills, understanding the physical world, social reasoning, memory, and so on. If the system falls short of typical human performance on any of them, it's not AGI yet. It has to clear the bar across the board, not just do brilliantly on a handful of benchmarks.

But a fixed test suite isn't enough, because people will always end up optimizing for whatever's on the list. So the second stage is adversarial. Once a system passes the battery, you give it to a team of people and say, "Try to find a cognitive task that a typical human can do and this system can't." If they search for a long time, really try hard, and can't find anything, then I think you have to say it's an AGI.

That second part is important, because current systems are very uneven. They can be remarkably good at things we find hard, like writing code or answering expert-level exam questions, and then surprisingly bad at things a child does easily, like certain kinds of spatial reasoning, or learning continually from experience and remembering it reliably over time. Those gaps are exactly where the adversarial testing will catch them.

I'd also stress that I mean the level of a *typical* human, not the best human in every field. Matching the best scientist or best mathematician in every domain is a much higher bar, more like superintelligence. To my mind, AGI is the point where you can no longer find those embarrassing holes, where it's genuinely general in the way people are.

r001.rationale: It defines AGI by whether a system can perform the broad range of cognitive tasks people typically can.

r002.rationale: It proposes a broad battery of cognitive tests and requires performance at least at the typical human level across them.

r003.rationale: It proposes deliberate adversarial searching for tasks typical humans can do but the system cannot, and says that failing to find any after sustained effort means it should be regarded as AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the term itself has always been a bit fuzzy, and I've spent a fair amount of time over the years trying to pin it down. The way I think about it comes back to the word "general." When we talk about human intelligence, we're talking about a system that can do a very wide range of cognitive tasks — learn new skills, reason about novel situations, understand language, plan, remember things over long periods, and so on. So AGI, to me, is a system that can do at least the range of cognitive things that a typical person can do, and can do them to roughly the level a typical person can.

Now, how do you actually judge that? I don't think there's one single test. People have proposed things over the years — the Turing test, various coffee-making tests, getting a degree, and so on — and each of them captures something, but each can also be gamed or turns out to miss important aspects. So my view is you want a battery of tests, a broad suite covering the kinds of cognitive abilities that cognitive scientists and psychologists have identified in humans: perception, memory, reasoning, learning, language, planning, social understanding. You want to cover that space as comprehensively as you reasonably can.

And then there's a second, more adversarial part. If a system passes all the tests you've written down, but someone can still come along and say, "Here's a cognitive task that most people can do, and the system clearly can't," then you're not there yet. So in practice it's a combination: a comprehensive test battery, plus the condition that people genuinely try and fail to find things humans can do that the system can't. When people stop being able to find those gaps — when the holes are no longer there — that's when I'd say we're at AGI.

I'd add that the human baseline matters, and I deliberately anchor on a typical person rather than an expert. Systems being superhuman in some areas is fine and expected — calculators were superhuman at arithmetic long ago. The interesting question is the floor, not the ceiling: are there still basic cognitive things people do that the system fundamentally can't? Right now, there clearly are — things like episodic memory, certain kinds of continual learning, some aspects of robust reasoning. So we're not there yet, but I think it's a judgeable question if you approach it that way.

r001.rationale: Defines AGI as handling at least the range of cognitive tasks a typical person can perform, at roughly a typical person’s level.

r002.rationale: Proposes a broad battery of human cognitive abilities and compares the system against the typical-person baseline.

r003.rationale: Says that if deliberate attempts can no longer find tasks most people can do that the system cannot, that is when to regard it as AGI.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we mean by general intelligence. The way I think about it is the ability to achieve goals across a wide range of environments. So the important thing isn’t whether a system can do one impressive task. It’s how broadly capable it is, and whether it can adapt when the task or the environment changes.

For AGI, I’d want to see a system that can perform at roughly a human level across a very broad range of cognitive tasks, including learning new things. You couldn’t establish that with a single test. You’d need a collection of evaluations, and you’d need to be careful that you were measuring genuine competence rather than familiarity with the questions.

A particularly useful test would be to give it something unfamiliar, explain what you want, and see whether it can learn how to do it. Can it use feedback? Can it recover from mistakes? Can it transfer what it has learned to a related problem?

There’s still a judgment involved, because ‘a broad range’ doesn’t specify an exact boundary. I’d expect us to have systems where reasonable people disagree about whether they count as AGI before we have systems where the answer is obvious.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI as performing at roughly human level across a very broad range of cognitive tasks, including learning new things.

r002.rationale: It proposes evaluating performance across a collection of tasks and says the system should perform at roughly human level across them.

r003.rationale: It does not propose that failing to find below-human tasks after deliberate effort is sufficient to count a system as AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by being clear about what we mean by general intelligence. The definition I’ve worked with is that intelligence measures an agent’s ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments. So you wouldn’t establish AGI by showing that a system is extraordinarily good at one thing. You’d want evidence that it can handle a broad range of tasks, including unfamiliar ones, and learn what it needs to succeed.

For a practical threshold, I’d ask whether it can perform at roughly the human level across most of the cognitive tasks that humans can do. That doesn’t mean it has to beat the world champion in every domain. But it shouldn’t have large, systematic gaps where an ordinary person can figure something out and the system simply can’t.

The difficult part is measuring that. A fixed set of benchmarks is never going to be entirely satisfactory, particularly if those benchmarks have become part of the training process. You need fresh tasks, you need to test adaptation, and you need to see whether the system can carry out something substantial rather than just produce a plausible answer to a short question. I’d expect the judgment to come from a collection of evidence, rather than one decisive test.

r001.rationale: It describes the practical AGI threshold as performing around human level across most cognitive tasks people can do.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing system performance with human performance across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

r003.rationale: It allows that there may be gaps, provided they are not large or systematic; it does not say that deliberate inability to find any below-human task is sufficient.
